questions.scenario: A consumer receives a record whose JSON can't be parsed.
questions.question: How should it be handled?
options: Retry it with exponential back-off for an hour
Skip it and log at debug level
Send it to the dead-letter topic at once, because no retry will fix it
Stop the consumer until someone fixes it
questions.explanation: Poison messages never succeed; mark the exception not retryable so it goes straight to the DLT.

questions.scenario: The SMS provider is down for 20 minutes. Notifications uses blocking retries with long back-off for every failure.
questions.question: What is the effect?
options: The partition stalls: every later event waits, and long processing can trigger rebalances
Nothing; blocking retries are free
Events go to other partitions
Kafka extends retention automatically
questions.explanation: Blocking retries hold the partition. For long outages, use retry topics or a shorter blocking window plus a DLT.

questions.question: What do you give up compared with blocking retries?
options: The dead-letter topic
At-least-once delivery
Consumer groups
Per-key ordering: later records with the same key can be processed while one waits in a retry topic
questions.explanation: Non-blocking retries keep the partition moving at the cost of ordering, which is fine when each key has one relevant event.

questions.scenario: Fraud and notifications both consume transfer-events and both use dead-letter topics.
questions.question: Why name the DLTs per consumer group?
options: Kafka requires unique names per service
So a failed record can be inspected and replayed to only the consumer that failed
To keep retention shorter
Because DLTs can only have one partition
questions.explanation: The same event may succeed for one group and fail for another; replaying it to everyone would be wrong.

questions.scenario: Records have been arriving in a DLT for three days and nobody noticed.
questions.question: What was missing?
options: A larger partition count
Kafka transactions
An alert on DLT records, an owner and a runbook to inspect, fix and replay
A schema registry
questions.explanation: A DLT without monitoring and a replay process is a slow way to lose data.

questions.scenario: A producer wants to rename amount to amountKobo in TransferReserved.
questions.question: What is the safe approach?
options: Add amountKobo, keep amount until all consumers have moved, then remove it in a new version
Rename it in one release
Change the type of amount to a string
Reuse amount with the new meaning
questions.explanation: Never rename, remove or retype fields consumers use; add, deprecate, then remove in a new version.

questions.scenario: A schema registry is set to BACKWARD compatibility.
questions.question: What does it guarantee?
options: Old consumers can read new events
New consumers can read events written with the previous schema, so you can upgrade consumers first
Producers and consumers can upgrade in any order
Schemas can never change
questions.explanation: Backward: new readers handle old data. Forward is the reverse; full is both.

questions.scenario: A message in the DLT came from a consumer bug that is now fixed.
questions.question: Why is replaying it safe even if it was in fact processed before?
options: Because DLT records expire
Because the replay tool deletes duplicates
Because the consumer is idempotent, so processing it twice has one effect
Because Kafka marks replayed records
questions.explanation: Idempotent consumers are what make replay a routine operation instead of a risk.
